2026 LOCAL ENHANCEMENT PROGRAMME 
On Friday, 5th December, Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht, Dara 
Calleary TD, and Minister of State with responsibility for Community Development and Charities, Jerry 
Buttimer TD, announced €7 million in funding under the Department of Rural and Community 
Development and the Gaeltacht’s Local Enhancement Programme (LEP) 2026. 
This funding will provide capital supports that are essential for many small community groups and 
organisations, particularly those who serve disadvantaged communities in rural and urban areas. It will 
be allocated across the local authority network. 
County Wicklow has received €199,043.66 as part of the Local Enhancement Programme 2026.  
There will be a particular focus on small capital works/improvements, and the purchase of equipment for 
community use. The funding may be used for but is not limited to; improving access for persons with a 
disability; enhancing community participation for disadvantaged and marginalised groups and improving 
energy efficiency of community facilities to reduce ongoing costs. 
The scheme is designed to ensure local priorities are identified and met, to improve and enhance 
community facilities for all. Funding will be available to a diverse range of community groups including, 
but not limited to, community centres, parish halls and local voluntary groups.

Housing Needs Assessment 2024 (SSHA 2024) 
 
The Summary Social Housing Assessment (SSHA) 2024 is the continuation of the ongoing process of annual

The purpose of the process is to identify the current level of national housing need. At county level, it captures the 
total number of households qualified for social housing support across the county whose social housing need is not 
being met, in order to understand the level of need for such support. The social housing applications were reviewed 
from 1st November 2023 to 4

Capital Assistance Scheme (CAS) 
Under CAS, the Department is accepting applications for capital funding for the delivery, through either 
construction or acquisition, of housing accommodation, to cater for priority groups including: 
• 
elderly. 
• 
homeless persons (including “care leavers” exiting State care on reaching the age of 18). 
• 
people with a disability, with particular emphasis on moving people with disabilities from 
congregated settings into community-based living. 
 
Assessment criteria 
CAS funding operates in partnership with Local Authorities and Approved Housing Bodies.  
Local Authorities assess the specific need for CAS funded housing being cognisant of the actual housing 
need of the CAS groups identified in the latest Social Housing Assessment, consultations with suitable local 
inter-agency/co-ordination groups that deal with special needs, such as the housing and disability steering 
groups, national policies and guidelines, including the National Housing Strategy for Disabled People.

Addressing Homelessness in Partnership with Approved Housing Bodies 
Homeless Supported Temporary Accommodation – Kilmantin Hill, Wicklow 
Kilmantin Hill has 11 rooms to support persons either homeless, exiting a higher support facility, or in danger 
of becoming homeless.  
There are 9 clients supported in the Kilmantin Hill facility, operated by Dublin Simon. There is continuous 
transition by the clients to suitable alternative accommodation. 
A report is being undertaken at present to cost the refurbishment of the current rooms with a view to making 
them all ensuite. More details will be available over the coming months. 
 
Homeless Family Service – Fitzwilliam Road, Wicklow   
Dublin Simon are engaged by Wicklow County Council to operate and manage the facility at Fitzwilliam 
Road, Wicklow as a Family Homeless Service. The building comprises of three 1-bed units, two 2-bed units, 
and two 3-bed units. Eleven families have now transitioned or are in the process of transitioning to a 
permanent home and the resulting vacancies are in the process of being occupied with families 
experiencing or in danger of homelessness. 
It is envisaged that families will avail of the service for circa 6-months STA (Supported Temporary 
Accommodation) with key working support to enable families to transition from homelessness into 
Homeless HAP, or alternative longer-term accommodation.   
Homeless Supported Temporary Accommodation – San Remo, Bray 
San Remo is operated by Dublin Simon and incorporates a service model whereby there are a number of 
emergency/cold weather initiative beds and Supported Temporary Accommodation Beds (STA). There is 
on site key working support linking in with clients.    
The Neighbourhood Liaison Committee is now operational and meets monthly.

the targets identified in the programme. Housing First recognises that a stable home provides the basis for 
recovery in other areas.  
 
Properties will be provided by both Wicklow County Council and Peter McVerry Trust for the implementation

Wicklow County Council has, to date, successfully accommodated 18 clients under Housing First.  Other

pending finalisation of sourcing of accommodation. The main issue facing this programme is the availability 
of 1-bed units in suitable locations with easy access to required services.

WICKLOW TRAVELLERS GROUP WINS AWARD AT THE ‘COMMUNITY OSCARS’ 
On Friday 7th November, a community group from Wicklow achieved success at the National Pride of 
Place awards held at the Limerick Strand Hotel in County Limerick.  
These annual awards, often referred to as the Oscars for community groups, celebrate the incredible 
work being done by community organisations across the island of Ireland.  
The Wicklow Travellers Group won silver in the Inclusive Communities category for their initiative titled 
‘Wicklow Travellers Urban Outdoor Programme,’ in partnership with the Wicklow Sports & Recreation 
Partnership. The project's goals were to encourage members of the Wicklow Travellers Group to engage 
with the outdoors through education, facilitation, and support.  
The group received glowing praise from the Pride of Place judges; “It was noticeable to the judges on the 
day of our visit that a strong sense of wellbeing was developing in the participants, and it was hoped to 
build on the skills learned through the project to contribute to the overall health, sustainability and 
wellbeing of the Traveller community.” 
Sponsored by IPB Insurance, the Pride of Place competition was established 23 years ago in 
collaboration with Co-operation Ireland to recognize the invaluable contributions made by volunteers and 
those involved in local community development.  
It has grown into the largest competition recognising community development achievements on the island 
of Ireland.

Transkribus, which renders handwritten records searchable —a significant advancement in the field of archives and 
records. 
 
The Shillelagh Board of Guardians was the governing body responsible for the Shillelagh Workhouse and the wider 
Shillelagh Poor Law Union, including public health, sanitation and rural housing. The Boards were initially dominated by 
the landed gentry, but increasingly included prosperous Catholic farmers and merchants by the end of the 1800s.  In 
County Wicklow the Poor Law Unions included Rathdrum, Baltinglass and Shillelagh, and the county was also served by 
the bordering Unions of Naas and Rathdown. 
 
The minute books contain the proceedings from their weekly meetings, which included the Workhouse Master’s report, 
numbers admitted, clothing for the inmates, disciplinary actions, staff and provisions. These records represent a rich 
resource for Irish social history, illustrating an early system of welfare, public health and social services, while providing 
detailed insights into the daily operations of the Guardians, their staff, contractors and the communities they served.

Professional Indemnity Insurance, is required to be submitted along with the application, confirming, to the satisfaction of 
the local authority, that the property is derelict i.e. structurally unsound and dangerous. 
To qualify for the grant, applicants must: 
Have proof of ownership or evidence of active negotiations to buy the property (that is, confirmation of engagement from 
the estate agent or owner of the property) where you are seeking approval in principle for a grant.

Live in the property as your principal private residence or make it available for rent. 
- 
Have proof that the property has been vacant for at least 2 years and that it was built up to and including 2007.

Change to Accommodation Policy for people fleeing the War in Ukraine  
From 10 November 2025 Ireland’s accommodation offering to newly arriving people fleeing the war in Ukraine will 
change.  
Under the revised approach, anyone fleeing the war in Ukraine, who registers for temporary protection and is looking for 
State-provided accommodation in Ireland, will be accommodated for a maximum of 30 days. They will be provided with 
food, laundry, other services and integration supports in Designated Accommodation Centres.  
People who stay in a Designated Accommodation Centre for 30 days will receive a reduced weekly allowance of €38.80 
per adult and €29.80 per child in respect of daily expenses, while they are resident in the centre. They will also be 
entitled to child benefit payments. When they leave the Designated Accommodation Centre they will be entitled to apply 
for standard social welfare assistance, equivalent to Irish citizens, subject to meeting the eligibility conditions.  
The focus of supports in Designated Accommodation Centres is on orientation on living and working in Ireland. During 
the 30 days, access to information such as how to source independent accommodation, pledged accommodation, 
employment, training, social welfare entitlements is provided.  
This revised approach to the accommodation offering has been adopted in order to respond to a recent large increase 
in the number of arrivals from Ukraine. This policy aims to ensure the State can continue to provide temporary 
accommodation to those most in need when they arrive.  
This change will not affect people who have already commenced their stay under the 90-Day Accommodation Policy, or 
those already availing of other State-supported accommodation. 
In addition to the above policy change, owing to a significant increase in arrivals and having regard to the need for 
prioritisation and equity, State-contracted accommodation will no longer be available to people who have previously 
held Temporary Protection in another Member State.
